metadata.title: Claude, Launch Review.
metadata.subtitle: What a Skill Actually Is
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Teardown register: does Claude gain sign-off authority when it picks up the launch-review skill? Take apart the mechanism — one folder, one SKILL.md, read top to bottom before Claude starts — and name the trade-off Anthropic made: repeatability at the cost of any judgment outside the file. Lands the carry-out that a skill is a checklist Claude reads before it starts, not new decision-making power.

beats.narration_text: Liam here, in for Bear. Hear that Claude has a launch-review skill and it sounds like Claude got sign-off authority — like it can greenlight a launch and the review meeting can stop. It didn't. Here's what a skill actually is, and what one file in a folder can and can't do.

beats.narration_text: That's the natural read. Say Claude has a launch-review skill and the word skill lands like a promotion — like Claude is now the one who signs the launch off, and the humans in the room can stop checking. It's a clean guess, and it's wrong.

Nothing in the model actually changed. Delete the skill's folder off the disk and Claude doesn't lose any launch authority — there was none there to lose. The one thing that goes out with the folder is a written checklist Claude used to walk through when the skill was called.

Here's what a skill actually is. It's a folder with one file in it — a plain-text SKILL.md. That file lists the steps of walking a launch through review, in the order they should happen, in the same English you'd use to brief a colleague. That's the whole thing. Not a model change, not a plug-in, not a permission — a document Claude reads before it starts.

When the skill runs, Claude reads that file top to bottom and works through it step by step, in the order it's written. No branching, no re-ordering, no shortcut — unless the file itself says branch. The order in the file is the order of the work.

That's what makes a skill a specification, not new judgment. The payoff is repeatability — same checklist, every launch, every time, no drift. The cost is scope — anything the checklist doesn't name, Claude has no special opinion about. They optimized for the same steps running twice; they gave up any adapting mid-run.

So launch-review never handed Claude the authority to approve anything. All it guarantees is that every time launch-review runs, Claude opens the same file and walks the same steps in the same order. That's the whole trick — and it's a real trick, but it's the one trick, not sign-off.

beats.narration_text: Which cuts both ways when you watch it run. Claude flagging every risk on the list doesn't prove it understood the launch — a checklist can be walked to the letter and still miss the thing it was never asked to check. And Claude flagging nothing doesn't prove the launch is clean — it may just be a case the checklist doesn't cover. The output is only as smart as the file it's reading.

So here's the carry-out. A skill named launch-review doesn't hand Claude sign-off — it's a written checklist Claude reads before it starts. The same steps run every time, which is the whole payoff. Anything outside those steps is still on you.

props.quote: A skill isn't sign-off — it's the same checklist, walked in the same order, every time. Everything outside the file is still on you.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's a prompt you can paste straight into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini — no code, no API. Pick one decision you already check the same way before every launch, and ask the model to draft you a SKILL.md for it: plain English, ordered steps, no branching unless you say so. Then ask it to read the file back to you before it runs — walk you through what it will actually do at each step, so you can catch the places where the checklist and the real check drift apart. Go deeper: which step in your file is really a judgment call the checklist can't hold, and where does that gap show up when the skill runs?

llm_exercise.prompt: I want you to help me write a SKILL.md — a plain-English checklist another AI can walk through before it makes one specific decision I already make the same way every time. First, ask me one question: what is the decision, exactly, and when do I make it? Once I answer, draft the SKILL.md as an ordered list of steps in the order they should happen, no branching unless I add one. Each step should be a single sentence someone could actually do. Then, before we call it done, read the file back to me and walk me through what you'll check at each step — not what the file says, but what you'll actually do — so I can catch the places where the checklist and the real check drift apart.
llm_exercise.dig_deeper: Go deeper: which step in your SKILL.md is really a judgment call the checklist can't hold — and where in the file does that gap actually show up when the skill is running?
